content.title: About
content.content: The bean burrito with no cheese is a Mexican dish consisting of a soft wheat tortilla filled with seasoned beans, rice, vegetables, and sauce. Cheese is omitted, making it lighter and suitable for those avoiding dairy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico where large wheat tortillas were used.
Beans in burritos are often cooked with tomatoes, onions, and spices for a rich flavor.
Leaving out cheese makes the dish more vegan‑friendly, especially when plant‑based substitutes are used.
Burritos are commonly served with guacamole, salsa, and lime for extra zest.
In the United States, burritos have become a fast‑food staple and appear on many chain restaurant menus.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide a substantial amount of protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from beans and vegetables supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Omitting cheese reduces saturated fat content, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Beans and whole‑grain tortillas supply B1, B6, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: The dish offers iron, magnesium, and potassium, supporting energy levels and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: High sodium in sauces
items.content: Prepared sauces can be salty; monitor sodium intake to avoid excess.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gas in sensitive people; soaking them before cooking helps reduce this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the burrito hot, cut in half for easy handling. Serve with salsa, guacamole, or a squeeze of lime. Vegans can add tofu or plant‑based cheese for extra protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Frozen burritos keep well for up to 3 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef enchilada is a classic Mexican dish consisting of corn tortillas filled with slow‑cooked beef, smothered in a chili sauce and baked until golden. The dish offers a rich, savory meat flavor with a hint of spice and aromatic herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “enchilada” comes from the Spanish “enchilar,” meaning “to coat with chili sauce.”
Traditional tortillas are made from masa (corn flour), though many modern recipes use wheat tortillas.
Mexico features several regional sauces: red (chipotle), green (tomatillo), and white (cream‑based).
Enchiladas are often served with rice, beans, avocado, and sour cream as side dishes.
The dish is commonly prepared for celebrations and family gatherings.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The beef filling provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Beef supplies heme iron, which is readily absorbed and supports oxygen transport.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Enchilada contains B12, B6, and niacin, which aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from sauce
items.content: Tomatoes and chili peppers add lycopene and vitamin C, offering antioxidant protection.

items.title: Fiber from corn tortillas
items.content: Corn tortillas contribute dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Beef and cheese can increase saturated fat intake; moderation is advised.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Chili sauces are often salty; people with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Chili peppers may irritate the stomach of those with sensitive digestive systems.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be allergic to corn tortillas.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve enchiladas hot, drizzled with extra sauce and topped with grated cheese. Common accompaniments include sour cream, guacamole, fresh cilantro, and a squeeze of lime. Eat with a fork and knife, cutting the roll into bite‑size pieces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat with a splash of sauce to keep them moist. They can be frozen for up to 2 months, wrapped tightly in plastic before placing in a freezer bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Vanilla ice cream is a frozen dessert made from milk, cream, and natural vanilla flavoring. It features a smooth, creamy texture with the characteristic sweet aroma of vanilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vanilla ice cream became a classic flavor in the United States in the early 20th century.
Traditional flavor comes from vanilla beans, but most commercial production uses synthetic vanillin.
Ice cream is stored at about ‑18 °C (0 °F) to maintain its structure and taste.
Slow freezing creates smaller ice crystals, enhancing the vanilla flavor.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream supply riboflavin (B2) and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Carbohydrates and fats give a rapid source of energy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience digestive discomfort.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Allergy to milk or cream requires complete avoidance of ice cream.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve ice cream in cups, cones, or bowls; it pairs well with fruit, berries, nuts, sauces, and baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ice cream in a freezer at ‑18 °C or lower. After opening, consume within 1–2 weeks to prevent ice crystal formation.

infant-formula-gerber-good-start-gentle-.title: Infant formula, Gerber Good Start Gentle, Stage 2 (353)

content.title: About
content.content: Gerber Good Start Gentle Stage 2 is an infant formula for babies 6–12 months old, formulated with partially hydrolyzed cow's milk protein. The blend includes prebiotics, DHA, ARA, and iron to support growth, brain development, and immune health during the transition from breast‑milk to solid foods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Designed for infants who need a gentler protein source than standard cow‑milk formulas.
Partially hydrolyzed protein reduces the risk of cow‑milk protein allergy.
Prebiotic GOS promotes a healthy gut microbiome.
DHA and ARA are essential fatty acids for brain and eye development.
No artificial flavors or colors are added.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: Provides a balanced mix of protein, fat, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals needed for infant growth.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA contribute to the formation of neural cells and visual acuity.

items.title: Gut health
items.content: GOS prebiotics stimulate beneficial bacteria, improving digestion.

items.title: Reduced allergy risk
items.content: Partial hydrolysis makes the protein less allergenic compared with intact cow‑milk protein.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Enriched with iron and vitamins A, C, D, which play roles in immune function.

items.title: Cow‑milk protein allergy
items.content: Some infants may still react; discontinue use and consult a pediatrician if symptoms appear.

items.title: Improper mixing
items.content: Over‑concentrated formula can strain the kidneys; follow the manufacturer’s mixing instructions.

items.title: Shelf‑life after opening
items.content: Use opened container within 48 hours and keep it refrigerated.

items.title: Iron overload
items.content: Excess iron may cause constipation; monitor intake and seek medical advice if needed.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Mix the specified amount of powder with warm (about 37 °C) water. Stir thoroughly until smooth, avoiding lumps. The prepared feed should be used immediately.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry powder in its original airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 48 hours and keep refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus) is a tropical vegetable also known as lady’s finger. Pickled okra consists of whole pods brined with vinegar, spices, and sometimes sugar. It has a characteristic sweet‑sour flavor, crisp texture, and bright green color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled okra is sometimes called “fried cucumber” because of its crunchy texture after brining.
In Southeast Asian cuisine it is served as a side dish with rice and noodles.
Fresh okra contains mucilage that aids digestion; some of this property remains after pickling.
In the United States pickled okra is popular in sushi rolls and seafood salads.
Okra is rich in vitamins A and C and antioxidants, making it beneficial even when preserved.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin A as beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is important for vision and skin health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Pickled okra is low‑calorie, making it a good option for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The brine can be salty, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to Malvaceae family
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to okra.

items.title: Preservative additives
items.content: Certain brands use preservatives; check the label if you are sensitive.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Some recipes include sugar, raising the product’s glycemic index.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled okra can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, rolls, or used as a garnish for meat dishes. Before serving, it is often rinsed to reduce excess brine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the jar of pickled okra in the refrigerator after opening. When kept properly, it retains flavor and quality for 2–3 weeks. Discard if you notice mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Yogurt made from low‑fat milk and mixed with fruit pieces is a light dairy product with low fat content and natural fruit sweetness. It is rich in probiotics, calcium, B‑vitamins, and also provides fruit fiber and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Low‑fat milk retains most nutrients while containing almost no fat.
Fruit additions often use seasonal berries and fruit chunks, boosting vitamin C content.
Probiotics in yogurt support gut health and strengthen immunity.
Low‑fat yogurt is a popular choice for athletes and weight‑conscious individuals.
In some countries yogurt with fruit is served as a dessert, in others as a light breakfast.

items.title: Rich in Probiotics
items.content: Probiotic cultures help maintain a balanced gut microbiota, improving digestion and immune function.

items.title: Low Fat Content
items.content: Low‑fat milk reduces the calorie density of the product, which is beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Calcium Source
items.content: Calcium supports strong bones and teeth and is essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Vitamins and Antioxidants
items.content: Fruit adds vitamin C, vitamin A, and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Yogurt provides high‑quality dairy protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Lactose Intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming yogurt, even low‑fat versions.

items.title: Milk Protein Allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey protein requires complete avoidance of the product.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Some fruit yogurts contain added sugar; choose unsweetened or low‑sugar options.

items.title: Canned Fruit
items.content: If fruit is canned in syrup, it increases the calorie and sugar load.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the yogurt as a snack, blend it into smoothies, use it as a base for desserts, or top with granola for crunch. Stir gently before serving to distribute fruit pieces evenly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the yogurt in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.
